items.title: Purism Is Crowdfunding the Librem 5 v2, a $1,599 RISC-V Linux Phone With Kill Switches
items.summary: The privacy-focused Linux phone gets a RISC-V chip, 8 GB RAM, a removable battery. Purism's new $1,599 Linux Phone can't match an iPhone on specs but that's not the point.
items.body:
If you have been following the Linux phone space for a while, you have certainly come across Purism. It is a US-based company that builds hardware as well as software with privacy and security as its sole focus.

Purism makes Linux laptops, phones, a security key, a VPN service and its own Linux distribution, PureOS. A signature feature across its devices is the physical kill switch. Flip this switch, and the camera, microphone or wireless radio is cut off at the hardware level. No software can turn it back on.

Back in 2017, Purism crowdfunded the original Librem 5. Almost a decade years later, it is back with its second smartphone crowdfunding campaign for the Librem 5 v2. And this time, it is running on RISC-V.

Key Specifications of Librem 5 V2

• Processor: Eight-core RISC-V SpacemiT K1

• Display: 5.7-inch, 720 x 1440

• RAM: 8 GB

• Storage: 128 GB, plus microSD (SDR104, 80 MB/s), bootable

• Rear camera: 13 MP

• Front camera: 8 MP

• Battery: 4500 mAh, user-removable

• Cellular: Improved 4G modem (5G planned for later), dual SIM

• Wireless: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth

• Ports: USB Type-C (charging), 3.5 mm headphone jack

• Smart card slot: Yes, with free firmware (chopstx)

• Hardware kill switches: Cellular modem, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth, microphone/cameras

• OS: PureOS (fourth release)

The phone costs $1,599 upfront, or $129 now plus $99 a month for 15 months.

The main change here is the processor. The Librem 5 v2 replaces ARM for an eight-core RISC-V SpacemiT K1 chip. RISC-V is an open instruction set architecture, which fits Purism's philosophy of controlling as much of the stack as possible.

But, there's a but here, Purism itself says RISC-V is not yet "drop-in and boot-up ready" for PureOS. Graphics, peripherals, ARM64 app compatibility, browser performance and power management are all listed as work in progress. You are basically funding that engineering work as much as you are buying a phone.

The rest of the hardware is modest at best. You get a 5.7-inch 720 x 1440 display, 8 GB RAM and 128 GB storage, with a microSD slot that can boot PureOS. The camera setup is a 13 MP rear and 8 MP front shooter.

Let me be honest here. At $1,599, you are in iPhone Pro and Galaxy S Ultra territory, and the Librem 5 v2 specs do not play in that league. The screen, the chip performance and especially the cameras are nowhere close to what flagship phones offer. If you want great photos of your dinner, this isn't your phone.

But Purism isn't trying to build a general-purpose flagship anyway. The target audience is people for whom privacy and data security matter more than specs: journalists, diplomats, activists, tech executives and people in sensitive lines of work. Basically, anyone who can afford to pay top dollar to keep their data their own.

On the privacy side, there are three hardware kill switches. One for the cellular modem, one for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and one for the microphone and cameras. The phone runs PureOS, and you don't need an Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon or Meta account to use it.

🇺🇸 US Manufacturing if Purism gets 5000 orders

Purism manufacturing facility in the US

Purism is also pitching this campaign to people who care about building technology outside the largest global supply chains (read China).

That only happens if the campaign reaches its 5,000-order stretch goal. At that point, Purism says the main PCBA (the phone's main circuit board) will be made at its own facilities in the USA, and potentially in the EU.

If US-made electronics are a must for you, Purism plans a Liberty Phone v2 "with Made in USA Electronics" following the Librem 5 v2 schedule. The current Liberty Phone already costs $1,999, so expect to pay even more for the "made in the US" privilege.

Why Pay a Premium for This?

I asked this question to the Purism team: "Why should anyone pay a premium price for a phone like Purism when a similar price can fetch them a top of the line product from Apple or Samsung with better hardware specs?"

Purism CEO Todd Weaver answered with a blog post. The crux of his answer is that you cannot put a price tag on digital freedom. Big companies spread their costs over hundreds of millions of devices, while a small company building a different kind of phone with less common parts naturally pays more per unit.

The other argument is that the money goes beyond the hardware. Purism says it invests millions into free software and PureOS, and that work is funded by the people buying its devices. In other words, you are paying for an operating system that gets developed and updated without ad revenue or data harvesting paying the bills.

He also widens the appeal beyond Linux enthusiasts:

"People who are curious about crowdfunding may want to see what a community-backed technology project can achieve. People interested in investment may want to explore a business with a clear social purpose. And people who care about U.S. manufacturing may want to know what it takes to build more technology outside the largest global supply chains."

That investment angle is real, by the way. The campaign has a "Contact me about investment" option starting at $5,000 for accredited investors. So if you can spend $5,000, you can become a shareholder (from what I understood).

Back the Librem 5 v2

The Librem 5 v2 is now live as a crowdfunding campaign on Purism's own website.

Support Librem 5 V2 Crowdfunding Campaign

The phone alone costs $1,599. If paying that in one go is too much, the payment plan lets you put down $129 and pay $99 a month for 15 months ($1,614 in total). That makes it a bit easier on the wallet.

The campaign aims for 2,500 orders and runs until February 15, 2027. At the time of writing, it had 101 orders. The first 250 backers get a Founders Edition with an Accessories Pack, and backers 251 to 500 get the Accessories Pack.

As for shipping, there's no clear date. Purism says the phone ships about 14 to 15 months after the campaign ends, which puts it somewhere in 2028 for regular backers. Beta units are planned for Q4 2027, and a DevKit (also $1,599) ships about 6 to 7 months after the campaign closes.

Should you back it? If you want to support alternative open source OS on phones, privacy and data ownership, and if you can afford it, this is one of the very few ways to put your money where your values are.

Just know that the user experience won't be mainstream. Some of your favorite apps won't be there, so those are some of the compromises you have to make.

But if you value your data more than a better camera, the Librem 5 v2 makes a case for itself. Am I right?

items.summary: Another Brick in the Paywall
items.body:
SPONSORED BY

Infisical

Your AI agents need API keys, but they shouldn’t hold them. Agent Vault brokers credentials at request time, so secrets never land in prompts or logs. Give AI agents access, not your secrets.

Newsletter Update: Software Previews

A few weeks ago, I stopped tagging AI-assisted projects in the newsletter as most projects now use AI in some capacity – and I can't be the arbiter of what is and isn't vibe coded.

This week, I'm adding hover previews (screenshots) to new software tiles in the web version of the newsletter. While not all vibe coded projects are identifiable by their design, many are – and so this will hopefully be the first of several tools deployed in the coming months to help you quickly judge for yourself which projects you'd rather avoid.

I'm adding similar functionality to the directory (which is also live today), but it'll take a few weeks to backfill existing apps.

Weekly Highlights

AI is ruining the internet. I haven't been shy in the past about my disdain for how AI has re-shaped online interactions, whether it's the influx of bot accounts on social media or the dozens of emails I receive each week that are all some form of the following:

Hi. I'm a big fan of This Week in Self-Hosted [sic] and thought you might be interested in a new project...

If it's a fit for the newsletter, great. If not, say the word and you won't hear from me again.

More specifically this week, though, I'm perturbed by how AI is closing off the open web after Reddit officially discontinued RSS feeds (they've been talking about it for months, but feeds finally stopped working this past Monday) and Last.fm announced API access will require a paid account starting in December.

Both of these announcements hit close to 127.0.0.1 given the number of platforms that rely on Reddit's feeds (mostly because of its dogsh*t interface) or Last.fm for the ability to scrobble streams from self-hosted music sources.

But as frustrated as I am with the changes, I can't say I don't understand them. Services are realizing that if they don't charge for their content, AI companies will happily profit off it for free.

If our goal was ever to create an open internet, we're officially moving backwards.

In other news and activity:

• Codeberg experienced downtime this week as a result of domain troubles that are still being sorted out with their registrar

• Two popular self-hosted projects were renamed – Hister (search) is now Nogon, and Edit Mind (video knowledge base) is now Orcah Studio

• OpenCloud announced they're restricting production releases to enterprise customers and limiting community users to rolling releases (similar to what Proxmox and others do)

• Infisical (disclosure: this week's sponsor) took some heat for paywalling custom roles in a recent patch release. Their founder responded to the backlash and acknowledged the lack of communication, but the paywall seems to be staying put.

• BookOrbit is scaring off third-party developers with restricted API routes, which the maintainer claims is to thwart cracked versions of the official app (please stop using this platform)

• NordPass released their annual report of the most common passwords, and (unsurprisingly) 123456 leads the pack (and apparently has for seven of the last eight years)

• FoxxMD, the maintainer of Multi-Scrobbler, is already working to help users migrate from Last.fm and needs some testers

• Redict, a popular fork of Redis created over licensing concerns, is being deprecated (and its maintainers are encouraging users to switch to Valkey instead)

• Wiki.js v3.0, which had been in development for years until its recent release, is somehow already on v3.5.0

• Manjaro Linux, a semi-popular Linux distribution, officially registered as a recognized non-profit in Germany

• Novel project ideas I stumbled upon: Turn DNS queries from ad-blocking platforms into a Galaga-style browser game; convert a tablet into a wall-mounted grandfather clock with notifications

Happy selfh.st/ing!

AI is ruining the internet. I haven't been shy in the past about my disdain for how AI has re-shaped online interactions, whether it's the influx of bot accounts on social media or the dozens of emails I receive each week that are all some form of the following:

Hi. I'm a big fan of This Week in Self-Hosted [sic] and thought you might be interested in a new project...

items.title: GrapheneOS Accuses Google of Kneecapping Android Partners With Pixel Exclusives
items.summary: The project also wants to talk to the DoJ and says it expects Google to start locking Pixel bootloaders.
items.body:
GrapheneOS has accused Google of leaning on phone makers to keep away from the project. The claim came in a thread on X today, where the project says makers were questioned about working with it, then threatened over their Google app licensing.

The project adds that courts have already found such licensing terms illegal more than once. It believes Google wants GrapheneOS limited to Pixel devices, the only phones the OS officially supports right now, with no other brand able to build on it.

What transpires in the sections below is what the project said, set against Google's documentation, the GrapheneOS usage guide, and a community list of compatible banking apps.

Google being called out

Google is sabotaging their OEM partners by making a growing number of features and updates exclusive to Pixels. At the same time, Google is trying to convince OEM partners not to support GrapheneOS or even bootloader unlocking. They're also trying to harm GrapheneOS directly.

GrapheneOS describes the pressure on phone makers as part of a wider push against independent Android builds.

The project says Google is working against GrapheneOS itself and expects it to go further. It sees Pixel bootloaders being locked down eventually and Play Integrity, an API it calls illegal, being pushed harder. And if that were to happen, Android forks would struggle to survive under that.

GrapheneOS believes some of Google's conduct breaks US criminal law and that antitrust violations can put individuals in prison. It wants to talk to the DoJ and says earlier cases against Google left its most serious violations largely untouched.

Supporters are being asked for introductions to prosecutors and regulators, with assurances that the project has the necessary resources to carry on no matter what happens.

Do they have a case?

GrapheneOS says more Android features and updates now stay Pixel only, leaving other hardware partners behind. Its examples are two of the four yearly major releases going to Pixels only and Android 17 QPR2 landing there first.

The same complaint came up over QPR1 in September.

It adds that partners are being steered away from supporting bootloader unlocking. Keep in mind that installing a different OS other than Android needs an unlockable bootloader.

A Motorola deal announced earlier this year is taking GrapheneOS beyond Pixels, with more Motorola phones expected soon. But there's an issue.

Google's pitches the Play Integrity API as a way for apps to check they are on a real, certified Android phone. With how GrapheneOS works, it inevitably runs into trouble with that. The OS is not Google certified, and that is what the API looks for.

GrapheneOS does not try to fake certification, as that approach would be fragile and need constant repair. It would rather apps use hardware attestation, a method it supports in full.

One more thing

Another recurring problem for the OS is how banking apps handle it. Many depend on Google Play services, and some turn away devices that are not Google certified.

GrapheneOS has kept chipping away at this. Earlier releases added a notification showing which apps use Play Integrity and an option to block it for apps that can run without it.

A later fix got a few banking apps working again after an update broke them.

The third-party PrivSec list gives a sense of where things stand. It is crowdsourced, covers banks from many countries, and was updated recently.

As an open source project, GrapheneOS is well within its rights to call out a company the size of Google over what it sees as malice. Whether any legal action follows is a story for another day.

items.title: Taking On Red Hat? Ubuntu Now Has an Official SysAdmin Certification
items.summary: Ubuntu is now offering certification exams, covering the basics of Linux to DevOps. The Academy launch also offers a 10% discount on these certification exams.
items.body:
Ubuntu launched Canonical Academy in October 2025. At that time, only one exam of its SysAdmin track was open to everyone. The rest were either in beta or were still being built.

That has changed now. Canonical has notified It's FOSS that all four exams of the SysAdmin track are live:

• Using Linux Terminal

• Using Ubuntu Desktop

• Using Ubuntu Server

• Using DevOps Principles

Pass all four and you get the Canonical Academy SysAdmin qualification.

The first exam costs $100 and every exam after that costs $125. That puts the full track at $475 if you take all four.

To mark the launch, Canonical is offering 10% off any exam with the code ACADEMY10, valid until January 10. You can pay for the exams from the Academy shop.

You take each exam online, in a browser-based Ubuntu environment. According to the exam guide, the exams are a mix of multiple-choice, scenario-based and hands-on tasks that you perform on a live system.

Man pages and the official Ubuntu documentation are allowed inside the exam environment, but you can't open other tabs. The exams are proctored through Proctor360, so you'll need a webcam, a microphone and a single display.

One thing to note here is that Chromium-based browsers are recommended for the exam and Firefox is not supported, which is a bit ironic for a Linux certification.

You can take the exams in any order. Each one runs between 75 and 120 minutes, and you get up to two retakes within a year.

Using Linux Terminal

This 75-minute exam is the foundation of the track, and it's where I'd suggest you start. It is also the easiest of them all, specially for beginners. It also gives you a good feel for how the hands-on exams work before you spend money on the others.

The exam covers moving around and manipulating files from the terminal, searching and modifying them with regular expressions, pipes and redirection. You also deal with system resources like logs and log rotation, cron jobs, and repairing partitions and filesystems with tools like fdisk, fsck and parted.

The security part covers SSH keys, users and groups, file ownership and permissions, password rules and sudo policies. This is absolutely mandatory Linux knowledge for any sysadmin, and you probably already know a good chunk of it if you use Linux daily. Still a certification exam is a good way to test your knowledge, specially when you cannot use internet or AI assistance.

Using Ubuntu Desktop

This 90-minute exam is more Ubuntu-specific. It covers installing Ubuntu, creating a bootable USB, upgrading between LTS releases, installing proprietary GPU and Wi-Fi drivers, and fixing boot problems with GRUB2 and initramfs. LVM volumes and snapshots are in there too.

A big part is application management, from apt and unattended upgrades to the difference between deb and Snap packages. You also get networking basics like configuring connections and layer 2 concepts such as MAC addresses and ARP.

The security section touches on PKI, file permissions with ACLs and joining an Active Directory domain. There's even a small section on the open source community, covering the LTS release cycle and Ubuntu's governance.

Using Ubuntu Server

This is also a 90-minute exam where the server side of things comes in. You are tested on deploying Ubuntu Server with PXE boot, autoinstall and cloud-init, and on booting into single-user mode.

You'll also manage services with systemd, set up automated backups with systemd timers or cron, run a file server with NFS or Samba, and put together a basic web app with Apache or Nginx and a database like MySQL or PostgreSQL. On the security side, there's SSH access and firewall setup with ufw or iptables.

Using DevOps Principles

This is the newest exam and also the longest, with estimated time ranging from 90 to 120 minutes. It covers automation scripts in Bash or Python kept in Git, and tools like cloud-init and Ansible.

You also work with containers and virtual machines using Docker, LXD and virsh. Patching through Canonical's own tooling, such as Landscape, Livepatch and Ubuntu Pro, is part of it.

The last section is about monitoring and troubleshooting, using tools like tcpdump, dig, ss and iproute2, and dealing with systems slowing down under load.

Why Ubuntu certification?

Ubuntu is not just a desktop distro. It's one of the most widely used Linux systems on servers and in the cloud, so it makes sense for Canonical to offer certifications for using its own system.

Red Hat has been doing this for years with its RHCSA certification and others. Ubuntu is late to the party, but better late than never.

It also strengthens Canonical's position in the enterprise world. A recruiter can now see whether a candidate can actually handle Ubuntu servers and systems. That could work as a requirement for entry-level jobs. It could also work as a way for employers to train their existing staff and improve their skills.

That said, keep your expectations real. The exams are not costly, but they are also not as in-depth as the Red Hat ones from what I see.

The badges carry the year of the Ubuntu LTS release the exam is based on. The current exams are based on Ubuntu 24.04, and the 2026 versions will move to 26.04.

There is no clear information on how long these certifications will be valid. I think it's two years, but that's just my guess.

As I mentioned earlier, use coupon code ACADEMY10 to get 10% discount. It's valid till January 10, 2027.

Canonical Academy

If you have been waiting for the full track before committing, now is a good time, especially with the discount running till January. Start with the terminal exam and decide on the rest after that. items.summary: Read what's happening in the Linux world, learn new tips and solve some puzzles in the latest edition of FOSS Weekly newsletter.
items.body:
After a gap of more than three years, Slax has shipped a new release based on Debian 13. It adds a graphical installer for USB or dual-boot setups, plus an AI helper that diagnoses and fixes system problems.

Manjaro’s developers have registered their own German nonprofit, the Manjaro Project e.V., which is independent of the company that has owned the distribution since 2019.

Dutch privacy-focused email provider Soverin has launched Soverin Suite, a managed workspace that combines email, files, documents, and video calls behind one login. It costs €10 per license monthly before VAT, with data kept in the Netherlands.

Canonical unveiled Surge at Ubuntu Summit 26.10, a multi-agent AI system that triages CVEs and writes backported fixes for Ubuntu userspace packages. Its fixes go to an opt-in Edge archive, not regular security updates.

Nextcloud has released Office Desktop, an open source suite with four editors for documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs. It runs on Linux, Windows, and macOS and handles both Microsoft Office and OpenDocument formats.

Two independent projects are working to bring MATE to Wayland in different ways. Polo, by developer Kerem Söke, builds a new compositor that keeps MATE’s current behavior, while MATE Wayland Desktop swaps Marco for the labwc compositor.

Firefox wants to hear your gripes about Microsoft, and it has a phone line for the job. Dial 1-855-25-FIREFOX and tell them what bugs you.

items.title: Now Nginx Has Critical Vulnerabilities
items.summary: The fix is out in version 1.31.9 and 1.30.7, and the oldest affected code goes back to nginx 0.5.33.
items.body:
nginx is an open source web server and reverse proxy that sits in front of apps and passes traffic to them, and it is one of the most widely used web servers around.

That kind of broad implementation is why a set of ten vulnerabilities fixed in nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 are significant; five of them even let attackers run code on a server.

The stable branch gets its fix in 1.30.7 and mainline gets it in 1.31.9; both went out yesterday.

Plus, most of the five only matter if a specific feature is in use. As a sysadmin, the first job you need to do is work out which ones match what your servers run.

The vulnerabilities

Each is a separate bug in a different part of nginx. nginx rates two of them as major and three as medium.

Its changelog says two of them might crash a worker process or have other impacts, with F5, the company that owns nginx, saying an attacker could run code under certain conditions.

F5 gives all five a 9.2 Critical score on CVSS 4.0. 📈

Two of them are in HTTP/2. CVE-2026-123007 is a memory bug in HTTP/2 flow control that goes back to nginx 1.9.5 and is rated major. If you didn't know, flow control limits how much data a server sends at once.

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free. That means the code keeps using memory after it has been released. It can happen in a worker process when HTTP/2 is in use and worker_connections is not enough. It is rated medium.

CVE-2026-121810 is the HTTP/3 one. It is another use-after-free with the same worker_connections condition, and it is rated medium. The affected range reaches back to nginx 1.25.0.

CVE-2026-123634 sits in the resolver and is also a use-after-free rated medium. It can happen when the resolver directive is in use and the same name is resolved at the same time in subrequests.

CVE-2026-113425 affects the mail proxy and only matters if you run nginx as one. It is rated major and has the oldest affected range of the five, starting at nginx 0.5.33.

F5's CVE records list NGINX Plus as affected too.

Protect your systems

The fix is to update to 1.31.9 if you follow mainline, or to 1.30.7 if you follow stable. Both are available from nginx.org.

The same releases also fix five other vulnerabilities, including an infinite loop while reading request bodies over TLS 1.3 that nginx rates as major.

items.title: Mysterium VPN on Linux is Strictly for Terminal Junkies
items.summary: The Mysterium VPN client is open source and works on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. It is command line option only, though.
items.body:
Using a VPN, or Virtual Private Network, on your computer hides your real IP address from websites and encrypts your traffic before it leaves your device, while your ISP remains clueless about your online activities.

It helps the most on networks you don't control, like public Wi-Fi at a cafe or an airport.

There are several VPN services that provide Linux clients. Mysterium VPN is one more name to consider, but its Linux client is a command-line tool, and there's no graphical app. But that's still fine for a seasoned Linux user, I guess. This also means that you can use the VPN on your headless server.

Mysterium VPN: Overview ⭐

Mysterium VPN is the work of MN Intelligence, a Vilnius-based company that specializes in consumer VPN services and home network tools. Mysterium VPN runs on a decentralized network where residential IPs come from independent node operators.

Those operators explicitly agree to share their home internet connections, and using Mysterium VPN never makes your own device part of the network.

The service also offers neat features like WireGuard support, hosting IPs, and a pool of 7,500+ residential IPs across 100+ countries. You also get city-level choices and residential IPs that are limited to the Plus and Pro plans.

Whichever plan you pick, the privacy policy pledges not to store your IP address, session data, or browsing history. Though I couldn't find an independent audit to back these claims.

The policy also lists session timestamps and bandwidth usage as data processed to run the service.

Using Mysterium VPN on Ubuntu

I tested v0.3.0 of the Linux CLI on Ubuntu 26.04 LTS using a Pro plan that Mysterium VPN provided me with access to.

Signing in starts with the sudo mystvpn auth command (I had messed up not using sudo on the first run). It prints a limited-time link that you open in your browser. 👇

Once you log in, the page asks whether to allow the Mysterium VPN Linux CLI access to your email address and subscription status.

When that was done, connecting to a server did not work at first. The client kept telling me to run the auth command again, asked for sudo repeatedly, and failed to save my sign-in state.

With sudo, the connect command ended in a permission denied error from wg-quick on one of the client's config files.

I contacted the developers, and they quickly sent me a set of commands to run. Together they add read access for the client's config folder to the AppArmor profile that wg-quick uses.

Creating the missing file:

sudo tee /etc/apparmor.d/local/wg-quick > /dev/null <<'EOF' /root/.config/mystvpn/wireguard/configs/ r, /root/.config/mystvpn/wireguard/configs/*.conf r, EOF

Reloading AppArmor:

sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/wg-quick

Verifying the file exists:

sudo cat /etc/apparmor.d/local/wg-quick

After that, the client connected without trouble and has kept me signed in across reboots.

Signing in, connecting, and disconnecting all need sudo, while listing countries works without it. Disconnecting takes sudo mystvpn disconnect, and running⁣ mystvpn on its own lists every available command.

For the speed tests, I picked Singapore since it is close to me but not the country I live in, and I ran Google's Internet Speed Test on a 200 Mbps Wi-Fi connection.

I started with a hosting IP. These come from data centers instead of home connections, and the client lists 55 countries for them. I connected with sudo mystvpn connect --country SG --ip-type hosting.

Download speeds stayed between 175.5 and 180.9 Mbps across three tests, while upload ranged from 2.72 to 141.4 Mbps, while some other attempts failed to complete. There was also some variation in which server I was being routed to, so that's something to keep in mind.

Next came a residential IP. These come from home internet connections, and the client lists over 100 countries for them. I connected with sudo mystvpn connect --country SG --ip-type residential.

Download speeds ranged from 17.8 to 79.6 Mbps across three tests, while upload sat between 0.08 and 19.3 Mbps. You can see that upload speeds swung widely on both IP types, and hosting gave the higher download speeds.

The gap was expected because data center connections are usually faster, and more consistent than a home connection. A residential IP makes more sense if a site blocks known VPN server addresses.

Normal browsing sessions were effortless, and I could access most popular websites with the usual CAPTCHA gates popping up accusing me of not being a human.

Configuring Mysterium VPN

First, ensure that you have all the dependencies required by the client. Then you can get the CLI installed on your Debian or Ubuntu system by using the following command:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/mysteriumnetwork/mysteriumvpncli/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash

There are also GUI apps for Windows, Android, iOS, and macOS, as well as a browser extension for Chromium-based browsers that can be downloaded from the official website.

Mysterium VPN

Ensure that you have an active paid plan before you configure Mysterium VPN on your system. Plans range from $2.99 for a Basic monthly plan to $93.36 for a two-year Pro plan. That's the Black Friday discount offer; otherwise, these numbers are more than double on usual days.

items.summary: Numbers don't lie (usually)
items.body:
SPONSORED BY

Infisical

Your AI agents need access to APIs and tools. How do you secure that access? Join our Nov 18 webinar on agent identity, permissions, and secrets, plus a live Agent Vault demo. Save your spot.

Weekly Highlights

If you missed it, I posted the results of the 2026 Self-Host User Survey this week (link below). Thanks again to all who participated – in total, it received 6,221 responses (a 52% increase from last year's 4,081 🚀).

2026 Self-Host Survey Results

With so many more participants than last year, it's difficult to tell whether certain shifts reflect real trends or just a different mix of respondents. Regardless, there were a number of results I found particularly interesting:

• The number of Portainer deployments has shrunk since last year and is now neck-and-neck with Dockhand – a platform that was only released earlier this year

• Debian and Ubuntu are wildly more popular than distributions like Fedora and Arch (this year's survey marked the first appearance of this question)

• 63% of respondents avoid vibe coded apps, 25% don't mind them, and 7% avoid AI-assisted projects altogether (the rest answered 'it depends' or 'other')

• Forgejo surpassed Gitea as the most popular self-hosted Git platform

• Proton Drive (storage) usage has grown significantly since last year (it'll be interesting to see how it makes out next year given its CEO's recent headlines)

• The number of laptop deployments has now surpassed that of server clusters

• 733 respondents are still YOLO'ing their application updates

• Three people who responded to the survey are over 80 years old (hell yeah!)

And lastly, everyone's favorite app this year was – well, you'll just have to find out for yourself.

In actual news and activity:

• Home Assistant continued their bizarre product naming habits with the announcement of the Connect AUX-2, a small box designed to bring smart home capabilities to non-smart devices

• Unraid's latest v7.4.0 release finally adds container template support for multiple custom networks and fields for memory limits

• An independent developer recently launched Vacuula, a custom server implementation for Neato robot vacuums, in response to the company's decision to phase out cloud services late last year

• Evgenii Burmakin, the developer of Dawarich, has launched a Discord for self-hosted software devs – send him a DM if you'd like to join!

• Verisign, a popular domain registry, confirmed it will grandfather existing .name domains after plans to completely discontinue the TLD stirred up some backlash a few months ago

• The world was introduced to Ram Altman, a satirical bash script that sends daily emails to Sam Altman when your machine has unused RAM

Happy selfh.st/ing!

Weekly Highlights

If you missed it, I posted the results of the 2026 Self-Host User Survey this week (link below). Thanks again to all who participated – in total, it received 6,221 responses (a 52% increase from last year's 4,081 🚀).
2026 Self-Host Survey Results

With so many more participants than last year, it's difficult to tell whether certain shifts reflect real trends or just a different mix of respondents. Regardless, there were a number of results I found particularly interesting:

items: The number of Portainer deployments has shrunk since last year and is now neck-and-neck with Dockhand – a platform that was only released earlier this year
Debian and Ubuntu are wildly more popular than distributions like Fedora and Arch (this year's survey marked the first appearance of this question)
63% of respondents avoid vibe coded apps, 25% don't mind them, and 7% avoid AI-assisted projects altogether (the rest answered 'it depends' or 'other')
Forgejo surpassed Gitea as the most popular self-hosted Git platform
Proton Drive (storage) usage has grown significantly since last year (it'll be interesting to see how it makes out next year given its CEO's recent headlines)
The number of laptop deployments has now surpassed that of server clusters
733 respondents are still YOLO'ing their application updates
Three people who responded to the survey are over 80 years old (hell yeah!)

blocks.text: And lastly, everyone's favorite app this year was – well, you'll just have to find out for yourself.
In actual news and activity:

items: Home Assistant continued their bizarre product naming habits with the announcement of the Connect AUX-2, a small box designed to bring smart home capabilities to non-smart devices
Unraid's latest v7.4.0 release finally adds container template support for multiple custom networks and fields for memory limits
An independent developer recently launched Vacuula, a custom server implementation for Neato robot vacuums, in response to the company's decision to phase out cloud services late last year
Evgenii Burmakin, the developer of Dawarich, has launched a Discord for self-hosted software devs – send him a DM if you'd like to join!
Verisign, a popular domain registry, confirmed it will grandfather existing .name domains after plans to completely discontinue the TLD stirred up some backlash a few months ago
The world was introduced to Ram Altman, a satirical bash script that sends daily emails to Sam Altman when your machine has unused RAM
